title: Serve roast potatoes with a serving spoon and fork
keywords: two tools, one in each hand
carrying loose food on a spoon
tipping food off onto a plate
instruction: Serve both roast potatoes onto the plate with the serving spoon and fork.
context: Serving food from a dish onto a plate with a serving spoon and fork is part of almost every family meal, and everyone has seen a potato roll off a spoon on the way. The two tools have to work together: the spoon is held tipped forward with its tip on the dish, and the fork pushes a potato up into its bowl, not under it. Then the spoon carries the potato over the dish's rim tipped back, so it rests against the bowl's back rim instead of sliding out of the open tip. Over the plate, the spoon tips forward so the potato slides off onto it. The food itself is never touched by hand.
setup: Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them; heights are above the table. Two arms (bases 61 cm apart), one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. (1) A white porcelain rectangular serving dish, 26 cm long (left to right) and 18 cm wide outside, 2.5 cm deep, walls 8 mm thick, about 1.5 kg, centred 33.8 cm forward and 7 cm left of the centre line. (2) A white porcelain dinner plate 24 cm across (its flat middle 19 cm across, the rim rising about 6 mm), about 0.55 kg, centred 33.8 cm forward and 18.5 cm right of the centre line, so 0.5 cm from the dish. (3) Two roast potato chunks in the dish, each a 40 x 30 x 26 mm block with its four long edges rounded (5 mm radius), about 30 g, lying flat with their 40 mm length pointing away from the robot. Their middles are 7.5 cm left of the centre line, 29 cm and 35 cm forward. (4) A 26 cm stainless steel serving spoon, about 110 g. Its bowl is 7 x 5.2 cm with low side and back rims and an open tip, and it balances 4.5 cm behind the bowl's middle. It rests bowl up in the dish's floor, the bowl's middle 33.8 cm forward and 1 cm left, its tip pointing left, its handle rising over the dish's right wall toward the plate. (5) A 27 cm stainless steel two-tine serving fork, about 90 g, with tines 7 cm long and 18 mm apart. It lies on the dish's left wall, its tines pointing right and raised, their tips 9.5 cm left of the centre line and 2 cm above the dish's floor, and the end of its handle on the table. Nothing else is on the table. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Measured at the end of the run, with everything still. 0.5 for each potato resting on the plate, its middle within 11 cm of the plate's middle, so 1.0 for both. 0.0 if a gripper touched a potato at any time (its fingertips' midpoint within 3 cm of a potato's middle), or if a potato fell onto the bare table at any time. In a real trial: a ruler from the plate's middle to each potato's middle, and the video for touches and drops.
reset_notes: Put both potatoes back in the dish on their marks, and lay the spoon and fork back in the dish as in the screenshot. Nothing is consumed: real trials use food-safe replicas of the potato chunks (printed or carved to 40 x 30 x 26 mm, about 30 g).
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1 with PhysX, 20 Hz control). The potatoes are rigid rounded blocks, and their friction (about 0.45) is estimated. The spoon's bowl is a flat floor with low rims instead of a curved bowl. Steel contacts take the lower friction, since polished steel is slick. The dish and plate are boxes and cylinders, and steam and gravy are not modelled. Cameras render at 320 x 176.
